hints: Look for a chloride that does not exist as a simple molecule, but joins together with another copy of itself to become more stable.
Recall that aluminium chloride exists as the dimer $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$, where each Al is electron deficient with only 6 electrons in its outer shell.
Think about how a lone pair from a chlorine on one $\text{AlCl}_3$ unit can be donated to the empty orbital on the other Al, creating dative bonds alongside normal covalent Al-Cl bonds.
walkthrough:
**Recall what each chloride looks like**

Think about the bonding type first. $\text{MgCl}_2$ is ionic, $\text{SiCl}_4$ is simple covalent, but $\text{AlCl}_3$ is special because Al is electron deficient.

$$\text{MgCl}_2 \text{ (ionic lattice), } \text{SiCl}_4 \text{ (tetrahedral covalent), } \text{AlCl}_3 \text{ (electron deficient)}$$

**Focus on aluminium chloride dimer**

A single $\text{AlCl}_3$ has only 6 electrons around Al, so two molecules pair up to form $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$. Each Al keeps its three normal covalent bonds to Cl.

$$2\text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$$

**Spot the dative bonds in the bridge**

In the dimer, two bridging Cl atoms use a lone pair to donate into the empty p-orbital of the other Al. Those two Al-Cl bridge bonds are coordinate (dative covalent), while the terminal Al-Cl bonds remain normal covalent. So both bond types are present.

$$\text{terminal Al-Cl = covalent, bridging Cl} \rightarrow \text{Al = dative covalent}$$

**Check Si and Mg**

$\text{SiCl}_4$ has four normal shared-pair covalent bonds and a full octet, so no need to dimerise. $\text{MgCl}_2$ is ionic with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so no covalent or dative bonds at all. Only statement 1 is true.

options.A: Incorrect. This would mean Al, Si and Mg all show both bond types. SiCl4 has only normal covalent bonds and MgCl2 is ionic, so they do not qualify.
options.B: Incorrect. This would include Si as well as Al. Si in SiCl4 already has a complete octet with four normal covalent bonds, so it does not form dative bridges like Al does.
options.C: Incorrect. This would include Si and Mg but exclude Al. This is backwards, as MgCl2 is ionic and SiCl4 is purely covalent, while it is Al that forms the dimer with dative bonds.
options.D: Correct. Only Al qualifies. Al2Cl6 contains terminal Al-Cl covalent bonds and bridging Cl to Al dative covalent bonds, where Cl donates both electrons. Well done for spotting the dimer trick.
